clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by mutations in PLP1 on the X chromosome; it lies at the mild end of the PLP1-related spectrum whose severe pole is Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease.
May be pure or complicated; complicated forms add nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria, cognitive impairment and diffuse central hypomyelination.
Missense and null alleles tend to produce the milder SPG2 end, whereas whole-gene duplication typically causes classic Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease, so dosage analysis is essential.
Early rotatory or pendular nystagmus and infantile hypotonia are important clues to the PLP1 spectrum even when limb spasticity dominates later.
A minor PLP1 isoform is expressed in Schwann cells, so some patients also have a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy alongside central signs.
Obligate female carriers may show mild spasticity, brisk reflexes or subtle white-matter change depending on the pattern of X-inactivation.
MRI in complicated SPG2 shows diffuse, symmetrical hypomyelination rather than active demyelination, which narrows the leukodystrophy differential.
reference.pathophysiology: PLP1 encodes proteolipid protein 1 and its splice isoform DM20, the most abundant proteins of central myelin, produced by oligodendrocytes, so the disorder reflects a graded, dosage- and misfolding-related oligodendrocyte dysfunction. Missense mutations cause abnormal protein to accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, triggering an unfolded-protein response and oligodendrocyte death, whereas null or loss-of-function alleles impair myelin compaction; the net effect is failure of normal central myelination (hypomyelination) with a superimposed length-dependent axonopathy that preferentially injures the long corticospinal and dorsal-column fibres and produces progressive spasticity. Expression of the minor DM20 isoform in Schwann cells accounts for the peripheral demyelination seen with some genotypes. Because the gene is X-linked, the underlying molecular lesion (duplication versus point mutation versus deletion) maps onto phenotypic severity, placing SPG2 at the milder pole and connatal Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease at the severe pole of a single spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal hereditary spastic paraplegias with white-matter change (SPG11, SPG15)
Spastic diplegia mislabelled as cerebral palsy
additionalInvestigations: Targeted PLP1 sequencing together with dosage analysis (MLPA) for duplication or deletion
Hereditary spastic paraplegia gene panel or exome sequencing if PLP1 is negative
MRI brain and spinal cord for diffuse hypomyelination and cord atrophy
Nerve conduction studies to detect associated demyelinating neuropathy
Brainstem auditory and visual evoked potentials
Carrier testing and X-inactivation studies in female relatives
Ophthalmological assessment for nystagmus and optic pathway involvement
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness or bulbar involvement suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Respiratory compromise in severe connatal presentations
Acute deterioration out of keeping with a slowly progressive leukodystrophy, prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: Highly variable; pure SPG2 may allow ambulation into adult life with slow progression, whereas complicated forms with early hypomyelination carry greater disability and overlap with the more severe Pelizaeus-Merzbacher end of the PLP1 spectrum.
pitfalls: Labelling a boy with spastic diplegia as cerebral palsy and missing the X-linked PLP1 diagnosis
Relying on sequencing alone and missing a PLP1 duplication that requires dosage testing
Assuming carrier females are always asymptomatic
Overlooking a coexistent peripheral neuropathy because central signs dominate
Confusing hypomyelination with demyelination on MRI and pursuing the wrong differential
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia and leukodystrophy review literature
